prize_parts.citation: for theories of firm heterogeneity and selection that transformed the analysis of exporting, reallocation and the gains from trade

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged from round 1: B044, Melitz and Helpman, as a single part. I re-tested it against the chair's questions and the exchange. Melitz (2003) put selection into exporting, productivity differences and within-industry reallocation into a tractable general-equilibrium model. Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple (2004) extended it to the choice between exporting and foreign direct investment. The result is one separable, citable discovery that changed the unit of analysis from the industry to the firm. It is more than twenty years old and has been taken to firm-level data in many countries, and its core predictions have been disputed mainly on welfare magnitudes, not on whether the mechanism exists. In answer to the chair's question on defining the award, I would word the citation around the theory of selection and the gains from trade. I would not claim the whole firm-level trade agenda. The omitted empirical and quantitative contributors (Bernard, Jensen, Eaton, Kortum) then sit outside the discovery, which I think is defensible, and I would not claim the boundary is uncontested. On adjacency, I think a neighbouring prize should count against a candidate only when the earlier citation covered the same discovery, and I apply that rule equally to B044 (2008), B038 (2021, 2023, 2024), B037 (2022) and B017 (2024). Under that rule the 2008 prize does not duplicate selection-based trade theory. I treat the count of supporters as no evidence of merit. B044 has the most explicit supporters, but it is still below six and I am not trying to build consensus around it. My case rests on credit clarity, maturity and distinctness. I also considered a multi-part configuration. I do not propose one, because B044 plus any other shortlisted part would name more than three people.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum made closely related empirical and quantitative contributions that a two-name award cannot credit, and Redding's quantitative extensions are left out. A second reservation concerns Helpman. Part of his broader reputation rests on trade theory close to the earlier work recognised in 2008, so his claim here must rest specifically on the firm-heterogeneity work with Melitz and Yeaple, and the citation has to say so. Third, the welfare magnitudes depend on functional-form assumptions such as Pareto productivity and CES demand. The qualitative selection mechanism is much better confirmed than the size of the gains. Fourth, trade was recognised in 2008, which some members may weigh for field balance, though I do not treat that as a scientific objection. Finally, B038 has the broader empirical footprint and speaks more directly to current debates, so it remains a serious rival on impact.

responses.point: Friberg also prefers B044 and argues that Eaton-Kortum is a Ricardian strand, less of a substitute for the Melitz mechanism than the Bernard-Jensen exporter facts. He would frame the citation around the theory of selection and the gains from trade, and he treats Redding as an extender.
responses.response: I agree with the framing and with Redding. I would add a limit to the Eaton-Kortum argument. It shows that the omitted Ricardian strand is not a substitute for the selection mechanism, but it does not show that its authors are undeserving. The honest position is that a two-name award recognises a theoretical discovery and leaves other real contributions unrecognised by design. That is a cost of the cap and not evidence that the discovery is poorly bounded. I also agree that a past prize is not a quota.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B044 first and separates the well-confirmed qualitative selection mechanism from the model-dependent welfare magnitudes. She words the citation around the mechanism, and she would credit Helpman here for the firm-heterogeneity work with Melitz.
responses.response: I share the separation and I have adjusted my citation to follow it: it now names selection, reallocation and the gains from trade, not a verdict on the size of the gains. I also agree on Helpman. His claim in this award should rest on the work with Melitz and Yeaple. I would not let his wider trade-theory record, part of which sits near the 2008 citation, stand in for it. Her point that she would support B038 if Dorn could be credited tells me the attribution argument is symmetric, and I take it as a warning against treating B044's cleaner boundary as costless.

responses.point: Andersson prefers B038 and answers my round-1 Autor-Dorn-Hanson proposal. He keeps Katz as the third name because Katz anchors the older skill-premium and education-versus-technology strand, and he accepts that this is a judgement call and that Autor-Hanson is an acceptable fallback.
responses.response: That is the strongest case for including Katz, and I do not dismiss it. It moves me from my round-1 view that the strands are hard to cite as one discovery to a smaller claim. A Katz version is defensible if the citation is written as one question about the determinants of labour demand. It does not resolve Dorn's claim, which remains direct on the China-shock papers. I do not change my own preference because of this. The Katz-versus-Dorn choice is exactly the unstable boundary that keeps B038 as my alternative and not my first choice.

responses.point: Hassler prefers B037 (Kiyotaki and Moore) for its clean two-name attribution. He accepts that the empirical validation of the channel is largely indirect and lists B044 as his first alternative, because he cannot resolve the missing empirical contributors from the supplied evidence.
responses.response: I accept that B037 has the cleanest attribution on the list, and that the 2022 overlap is adjacency and not duplication. Applying my adjacency rule consistently, I should not hold the 2022 prize against it as strongly as I did in round 1. What still keeps it below B044 for me is the empirical side that you concede. The collateral channel has disciplined a large quantitative literature, but direct micro evidence for the specific amplification mechanism is thinner than the firm-level confirmation of selection in trade. That is a weighting difference. B044's own uncertainty, the uncredited empirical contributors, is real, and I cannot say it is smaller than the B037 uncertainty.

responses.point: Boppart prefers B038 and says that if the committee splits the technology and trade strands, Dorn should displace Katz in the trio. He also says the selection mechanism in B044 builds on the 2008 prize and does not duplicate it, and he treats Redding as later work.
responses.response: I agree on Dorn if the strands are split, and that is what I proposed in round 1. I also agree on Krugman and Redding. We differ on whether the labour-demand programme is one discovery, and I have not found a way to settle that from the evidence in the files. I will flag a limit on my own judgement. My work on capital-skill complementarity is adjacent to B038, and I should not let that familiarity push me toward or away from it. For that reason I give B038 no more weight than I would a candidate outside my field, and I treat my alternatives as unranked by closeness to my own work.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a two-name award defined around the theory of selection and the gains from trade, when Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum (and arguably Redding) fall outside it.
How much of Helpman's claim rests on the firm-heterogeneity work with Melitz and Yeaple and how much on a wider trade-theory record close to the 2008 citation.
How sensitive the gains-from-trade magnitudes are to Pareto and CES assumptions.

If B044 cannot reach six votes, I would accept B038 as the fallback, though I have not settled whether the labour-demand programme is one discovery or two, or whether the third name should be Katz or Dorn. Katz would require a citation that states which of his contributions it recognises, since he also appears on B045.
Whether B017 is the right second alternative. Besley's inclusion is unsettled, and I have not resolved the overlap with the 2024 prize or the cross-country identification concerns.
I have not independently verified citation or impact figures, the 2022 scientific background, or priority claims. These rest on my own knowledge and on colleagues' statements.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. The supplied profile lists no co-authorship or institutional tie to Melitz or Helpman (B044), nor to the credited names on my alternatives B038 and B017. I have co-authored with fellow members Timo Boppart and John Hassler, and I am the committee's secretary, so I disclose these ties and the secretary role without treating them as evidence of merit. My work on capital-skill complementarity and inequality is adjacent to B038, and my work on the political economy of growth is adjacent to B017. I have also read Jan Teorell's disclosure about the co-author named only Persson, and I cannot resolve it from my own materials. In the chair's question about limiting participation, I know of no disclosed tie that would require me to limit mine. Conflicts are disclosed and not adjudicated.
